title: A Conservator on Tape
passage:
The certificate came in wrapped in a tea towel, torn across in about 1974 and mended at home with a strip of clear tape. Three flakes of film clung at one edge; the rest was a hard brown band the width of the strip.

“People ask me to take the tape off,” says Odette Fenniscarth, a paper conservator. “Mostly there’s no tape left; the film let go years ago. What’s left is the glue. The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown – and the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it.”

“Tape holds a tear for ten years and marks the sheet for a hundred. A mend from last year I warm, and the film lifts and brings most of the glue with it. One like this, heat won’t shift. The glue’s gone hard, so it’s solvent, and which solvent depends on what the glue was made of. The brown that’s in the fibres I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.”

– Oscar Goddard

questions.prompt: What does Fenniscarth say about mends made with clear tape?

options.text: The brown along the tear is plasticiser that has oxidised since the film came away.
Heat is for mends whose adhesive has hardened, and solvent for those still soft.
Where the adhesive gets into the paper, the sheet turns translucent enough to read through.
Once the solvent is matched to the adhesive, the brown comes out of the fibres with it.

questions.rationale: Option C is the key. It paraphrases the conservator’s own account of what the adhesive does to the sheet: “the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper. Where the glue went in, the sheet’s gone like greased paper; you can read the back through it.” Greased paper lets light through, and being able to read the back of a sheet through the stained area is what translucent means, so C restates the passage’s mechanism in other words without lifting any run of them. It is a specific, checkable detail, not a summary of the piece. Option A tempts because it reuses two things the passage really says – that the glue has oxidised and that the film came away – and reassigns them: it makes the plasticiser the thing that has turned brown. The passage says the opposite in one sentence: “The rubber in it has oxidised – that’s the brown – and the plasticiser that kept it soft has soaked into the paper.” The brown is the oxidised rubber; the plasticiser is the part that went into the sheet. A reader who has not sorted the two components will find A natural, which is why it has to be checked against that sentence. Option B swaps her two methods. She warms a young mend so that the film lifts and takes most of the glue with it, and she turns to solvent once the glue has gone hard: “One like this, heat won’t shift. The glue’s gone hard, so it’s solvent.” B gives heat to the hardened glue and solvent to the soft, which is the reverse pairing. Everyday experience that warmth softens hard things makes the swap sound right, and the passage is explicit that on a mend of this age heat gets nowhere. Option D overshoots what she promises. Matching the solvent to the glue is in the passage (“which solvent depends on what the glue was made of”), but the outcome D attaches to it is not: of the brown already in the fibres she says “I can lighten. I don’t promise to take it out.” D turns a limited result into a complete one. None of A, B or D is true as written, so the question does not turn on a best fit; each fails against a sentence a careful reader can point to.

mechanism_verification_note.direction_check: Every arrow in the passage runs the documented way: oxidation -> browning of the rubber; plasticiser -> into the paper -> translucency; adhesive loses tack -> carrier detaches while residue stays; young/tacky -> heat lifts carrier; crosslinked/hard -> solvent; stain in fibres -> reducible, not reliably removable. 'Clear tape' on a 1974 home mend is period-correct for a cellulose-film carrier with a rubber-based adhesive, which is the adhesive class that browns.
